subject: 🌀 Mixed market signals
body_html:
Plus: Fiscal milestone | Thursday, August 20, 2026
 
View in browser
 
 
Axios Macro
By Neil Irwin and Courtenay Brown · Aug 20, 2026

🎢 What went down is coming right back up: Long-term borrowing costs are surging again this morning, wiping out yesterday's decline.

  • In today's edition, we look at how Treasury's bond market intervention exposed a tension with the Warsh-era Fed's approach to financial markets.
  • Plus, a new milestone and a reminder of Washington's grim fiscal outlook.

Situational awareness: Initial jobless claims fell by 6,000, to 206,000, last week, near historically low levels that suggest employers remain reluctant to lay off staff.

Today's newsletter, edited by Jeffrey Cane and copy edited by Katie Lewis, is 821 words, a 3-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: Washington's market contradiction
 

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh. Photo illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Photos: Shawn Thew/EPA/Bloomberg and Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images
 

Kevin Warsh is trying to unwind years of explicit Federal Reserve guidance. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent may have just complicated that experiment.

Why it matters: While the Federal Reserve chairman wants to give markets more room to respond to the economy, Treasury's intervention signals that there are limits to how much market-driven movement Washington is willing to tolerate.

  • The result is a contradictory policy mix: The Fed is trying to do less to guide financial markets, just as Treasury is showing a greater willingness to intervene when market moves become uncomfortable.

What they're saying: "We are in a regime where activist Treasury policy is as material — for good and for bad — as central bank policy," Krishna Guha, Evercore ISI vice chairman, wrote in a client note this morning.

  • "Warsh has tried to make the unconventional case that the Fed should stand back" and allow markets to determine the level of interest rates needed to restrain the economy, Guha noted.
  • But "it is hard to make that case" when investors see Bessent seeking to influence long-term rates.

Driving the news: Treasury yesterday said it would double the size of its long-term debt buybacks, providing some relief from a sell-off that had pushed the 30-year yield to its highest level since 2007.

  • In an interview with CNBC this morning, Bessent emphasized Treasury's room to do more, including increasing buybacks beyond $4 billion per issue.
  • "We have a big toolkit, so we'll see," he said.
  • Bessent said the intervention was partly about "signaling" that Treasury believes yields don't reflect the economy's underlying fundamentals.

Flashback: At last month's Fed press conference, Warsh said that the rise in long-term interest rates showed investors were responding more independently to the economic outlook.

  • "Market participants are learning to play the ball, not the referee," he said.
  • "Market prices will continue to respond in the direction and magnitude they see fit. This is, in my view, a change for the better — and we're just getting started."

By the numbers: The sell-off in long-term bonds intensified afterward, although Warsh's comments were far from the only factor.

  • The 30-year yield jumped from 5.09% the day before the Fed decision to 5.21% the next morning, and kept climbing in the weeks that followed to touch the highest level since 2007.

The intrigue: The relief brought by yesterday's Treasury move was fleeting, as economists anticipated.

  • The yield on the 30-year bond was around 5.25% this morning, essentially where it was before Treasury stepped in.

What to watch: While Warsh has embraced a greater role for markets in determining financial conditions, Bessent has made lowering borrowing costs a central part of the Trump administration's affordability agenda.

  • That tension is clear when long-term yields jump up. What the Fed sees as a market signal translates into higher borrowing costs for households and businesses, worsening the affordability problem that administration officials are trying to address.

The bottom line: Warsh wants investors focused on the economy rather than signals from Washington, though Treasury's action gives markets a new reason to keep watching Washington.

2. $40 trillion milestone
 
Data: U.S. Treasury; Chart: Danielle Alberti/Axios

The chart above shows one key reason yesterday's decline in borrowing costs from the intervention announcement didn't stick.

  • Federal debt crossed the largely symbolic $40 trillion mark this week, an especially fitting milestone amid the turmoil in long-term bonds.

Why it matters: Treasury can intervene in the bond market. But the U.S. government's enormous deficits and borrowing needs remain.

What they're saying: "A ballooning deficit that has little-to-no-prospects of going away has had a hand in driving yields higher," Hardika Singh, an economic strategist at Fundstrat Research, wrote in a note this morning.

  • "[M]aking yields go down over the longer period will require the painful work of bringing down the debt," Singh added.

What to watch: Bessent told CNBC this morning that there is "a very good chance we have" seen peak deficits of the Trump administration.

  • Bessent pointed to tariff refunds as a temporary factor widening the deficit, with tariff revenue expected to resume as tariffs come back into effect.

By the numbers: The government ran a $1.8 trillion deficit last year and is on track for another roughly $2 trillion shortfall in 2026, according to the Congressional Budget Office.

  • Persistent deficits mean Treasury will have to keep adding to that $40 trillion debt pile at a time when long-term borrowing costs are near multidecade highs.
